title: 6 Samples and Uncertainty
text:
Last week, we described NO2 levels for all 4,994 LSOAs in London. In practice, however, we hardly ever have data for everything. Air pollution is only measured at a few hundred monitoring sites across London, and the values in our dataset come from a model that fills in the gaps. Similarly, surveys ask a few thousand people rather than the whole country. The question we usually face is therefore: if we only have a sample, how close are we to the truth, and how sure can we be?
Because our dataset covers every LSOA in London, we are in the unusual position of knowing the true answer. This week, we will treat the full dataset as the population, draw samples from it, and see how close these samples get.






ImportantBefore the session



Open the GEOG0187-stats project you created in Session 5 and create a new script called w06-uncertainty.R.




Before we start, it is important to distinguish between two terms:

A parameter describes the population, for example the mean NO2 across all 4,994 LSOAs. A parameter is fixed, but usually unknown.
A statistic describes a sample, for example the mean NO2 in the 30 LSOAs we happened to measure. A statistic is known, but changes from one sample to the next.

We use statistics to estimate parameters. Let us start by loading the data and storing the true mean, which in real research we would not know:



R code

# load the tidyverse and the data
library(tidyverse)
lsoa <- read_csv('data/london-lsoa-air-quality.csv')

# the population mean: normally unknown!
true_mean <- mean(lsoa$no2)
true_mean


[1] 21.74612





Suppose we can afford air quality monitors in 30 LSOAs, selected at random. We can use slice_sample() to pick 30 random rows from our dataset. Because the selection is random, we first fix R’s random number generator with set.seed(). This makes sure that we get the same sample every time we run the script:



R code

# fix the random numbers (try your own number too)
set.seed(48)

# a random sample of 30 LSOAs
my_sample <- lsoa |>
  slice_sample(n = 30)

# the sample mean: our estimate of the true mean
mean(my_sample$no2)


[1] 21.30667


Our estimate is close to the true mean, but not exactly the same.






NoteTry it yourself



Change 48 to any other number, run the lines again, and compare your result with your neighbour’s.


Everyone will get a slightly different estimate. This variation from one sample to the next is called sampling variability, and it is what the rest of this session is about.



What happens if we repeat the whole exercise 1,000 times? We can do this with replicate(), which runs a piece of code many times and collects the results. Here we use base R’s sample() function, which draws random values from a single column:



R code

# 1,000 samples of 30 LSOAs, keeping the mean of each
set.seed(48)
sample_means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(lsoa$no2, 30)))

# the first few sample means
head(sample_means)


[1] 21.30667 22.23000 21.86000 21.73333 22.78667 21.72000


The distribution of all these sample means is called the sampling distribution.






NotePredict first



Where do you expect the 1,000 sample means to be centred, and will they be more or less spread out than the NO2 values of individual LSOAs in last week’s histogram?


Let us plot the sample means, together with the true mean:



R code

hist(sample_means, breaks = 30,
     main = 'Sampling distribution of the mean (n = 30)',
     xlab = 'Sample mean NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Number of samples',
     col = 'grey80', border = 'white')
abline(v = true_mean, lty = 2)








Figure 1: Means of 1,000 random samples of 30 LSOAs. The dashed line is the true mean.





There are three things to notice here:

The sample means are centred on the true mean: on average, a random sample gets it right.
Individual samples miss the true mean by a little, in either direction.
The distribution is bell-shaped, even though NO2 itself is somewhat skewed (have a look back at last week’s histogram). This is known as the central limit theorem.




The spread of the sampling distribution tells us how far a typical sample mean is from the true mean. The standard deviation of the sampling distribution has its own name: the standard error (SE).



R code

# standard error: the sd of the sample means
sd(sample_means)


[1] 0.567464


In real research, we cannot draw 1,000 samples: we only have one. Fortunately, we can estimate the standard error from that single sample:
\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
where \(s\) is the standard deviation in the sample and \(n\) is the sample size. Let us apply this to our sample:



R code

# standard error estimated from one sample
sd(my_sample$no2) / sqrt(30)


[1] 0.4820915


The two values are close, which means that a single sample is enough to tell us roughly how precise our estimate is.






Be careful not to confuse the standard deviation with the standard error. The standard deviation describes how much LSOAs differ from each other. The standard error describes how much a sample mean would vary from one sample to the next. Collecting more data does not make LSOAs more alike, but it does make our estimate of their mean more precise.






How does the standard error change with the size of the sample? We can find out by repeating our simulation for samples of 10, 30, 100 and 300 LSOAs.






NotePredict first



A sample of 300 LSOAs is ten times larger than a sample of 30. Do you expect its standard error to be ten times smaller?





R code

# simulated standard error for different sample sizes
set.seed(48)
sizes <- tibble(n = c(10, 30, 100, 300)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(se = sd(replicate(1000, mean(sample(lsoa$no2, n))))) |>
  ungroup()
sizes


# A tibble: 4 × 2
      n    se
  <dbl> <dbl>
1    10 1.02 
2    30 0.592
3   100 0.328
4   300 0.186


The standard error becomes smaller as the sample gets larger, but only slowly: we need four times as many LSOAs to halve the standard error. This is the effect of the \(\sqrt{n}\) in the formula, and it is why precision is expensive.



A sample mean on its own hides how uncertain it is. A confidence interval (CI) makes this uncertainty visible. Because the sampling distribution is bell-shaped, about 95% of sample means fall within 1.96 standard errors of the true mean. Turning this around, we can calculate a 95% confidence interval as:
\[
\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \times SE
\]



R code

# 95% confidence interval from our one sample
m <- mean(my_sample$no2)
se <- sd(my_sample$no2) / sqrt(30)
c(lower = m - 1.96 * se, upper = m + 1.96 * se)


   lower    upper 
20.36177 22.25157 


R can also calculate this for us with the t.test() function. This uses a slightly larger multiplier than 1.96, taken from the t distribution, to allow for the fact that \(s\) is itself estimated from a small sample. As a result, the interval is a little wider:



R code

# the same, from t.test()
t.test(my_sample$no2)$conf.int


[1] 20.32068 22.29265
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95




The 95% does not mean that there is a 95% chance that the true mean lies within your interval: the true mean is fixed, and your interval either contains it or it does not. Instead, it means that the method captures the true mean in 95% of samples. Because we know the true mean, we can check this. Let us draw 100 samples, calculate a confidence interval for each of them, and count how many contain the true mean.






NotePredict first



Before you run the code, write down how many of the 100 intervals you expect to contain the true mean.





R code

# 100 samples, a 95% CI for each
set.seed(48)
ci_sim <- tibble(sample_id = 1:100) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(values = list(sample(lsoa$no2, 30)),
         mean = mean(values),
         se = sd(values) / sqrt(30),
         lower = mean - 1.96 * se,
         upper = mean + 1.96 * se) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(hit = lower <= true_mean & upper >= true_mean)

# how many intervals contain the true mean?
sum(ci_sim$hit)


[1] 94


We can also plot all 100 intervals:



R code

# plot the intervals: grey = contains the true mean, red = misses
plot(NULL, xlim = range(ci_sim$lower, ci_sim$upper), ylim = c(1, 100),
     main = '100 confidence intervals',
     xlab = 'NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Sample')
segments(ci_sim$lower, ci_sim$sample_id, ci_sim$upper, ci_sim$sample_id,
         col = ifelse(ci_sim$hit, 'grey40', 'red'))
abline(v = true_mean, lty = 2)








Figure 2: 95% confidence intervals from 100 samples of 30 LSOAs. Red intervals miss the true mean (dashed line).





Roughly 95 out of 100 intervals contain the true mean. In real research, however, we never know whether our interval is one of the unlucky ones.




So far, we have assumed that our sample is random. Suppose instead that all monitors were placed in Inner London, for instance because that is where pollution is expected to be highest:



R code

# a sample of 30 LSOAs from Inner London only
set.seed(48)
inner_sample <- lsoa |>
  filter(inner_outer == 'Inner') |>
  slice_sample(n = 30)

# 95% CI from this sample, and the true London mean
t.test(inner_sample$no2)$conf.int


[1] 24.41852 26.87481
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95

true_mean

[1] 21.74612


The interval looks just as precise as before, but it is in the wrong place. Taking a larger sample from Inner London would make the interval narrower, but it would still be wrong. Confidence intervals capture random error (sampling variability), but not bias: systematic error caused by how the data were collected. This is why the question of how a sample was selected should always come before any calculation.






NoteTry it yourself



Change 'Inner' to 'Outer' in the code above. Before you run it, predict whether the interval will be too high or too low, and then check.








Think back to your fieldwork. Were your survey sites a random sample of the area? What would a confidence interval based on these sites tell you, and what would it not tell you?






When you report an estimate based on a sample, for instance in an essay or a worksheet, you should report its uncertainty alongside it, explain how the sample was drawn, and interpret the interval in plain words. Based on this session’s sample, this could look as follows:

In a random sample of 30 London LSOAs, mean annual NO2 was 21.3 µg/m³ (95% CI 20.3 to 22.3 µg/m³). Values for London as a whole between these two numbers are consistent with our sample.

Avoid writing that there is a “95% probability” that the true mean lies in your interval (see What does 95% mean?).






NoteTry it yourself



Do the same for PM2.5: draw a random sample of 30 LSOAs, report the mean with its 95% confidence interval, and check whether your interval contains the true mean.





By the end of this session, you should have:

saved your script as w06-uncertainty.R;
explained, in your own words, the difference between a parameter and a statistic, and between a standard deviation and a standard error;
plotted a sampling distribution, and calculated the standard error by simulation and with the formula;
calculated a 95% confidence interval from one sample, and plotted 100 intervals;
explained in one or two sentences why a confidence interval cannot fix a biased sample;
reported a PM2.5 estimate with its confidence interval.











Problem
What to try




My numbers differ from the page
Check that you ran set.seed(48) directly before the line that draws the sample. Any other seed gives different, equally valid, numbers.


object 'true_mean' not found
Run your script from the top: later lines depend on earlier ones.


The simulation takes a while
1,000 repetitions takes a second or two. If it hangs, use Session → Interrupt R and check for typos.

title: 7 Testing Differences
text:
We previously found that more deprived LSOAs tend to have somewhat higher levels of NO2. Last week, we saw that a sample never matches the population exactly. This week, we bring the two together. When we see a difference between two groups in a sample, how do we know whether it reflects a real difference in the population, or whether it could simply be the result of which LSOAs happened to end up in our sample? This is the question a hypothesis test tries to answer.
You already ran a t-test in Term 1. This week, we will look at what such a test actually does, what its result does and does not tell us, and how to report it. This session links to the second statistics worksheet, so you can use the time in class to make a start on your own analysis.






ImportantBefore the session



Open your GEOG0187-stats project. Create a new script, w07-testing.R. Have a look back at Confidence intervals from last week.




We also found that the link between income deprivation and NO2 looked different in Inner and Outer London. In this session, we will focus on Outer London and look at whether LSOAs in the most income-deprived fifth of London are exposed to higher levels of NO2 than LSOAs in the least deprived fifth.
Just like last week, we will pretend that we cannot measure every LSOA and instead only have data for a random sample: in this case, 30 LSOAs from each group. Because we do in fact have data for all LSOAs, we can check at the end how close our sample got to the true answer.
Let us start by loading the data, adding the income deprivation quintiles we created before, and selecting the two groups we want to compare:



R code

# load the tidyverse and the data
library(tidyverse)
lsoa <- read_csv('data/london-lsoa-air-quality.csv')

# income deprivation quintiles across London, as before
lsoa <- lsoa |>
  mutate(income_quintile = ntile(income_score, 5))

# Outer London, least (1) and most (5) deprived fifths only
outer <- lsoa |>
  filter(inner_outer == 'Outer', income_quintile %in% c(1, 5)) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(income_quintile == 5, 'Most deprived', 'Least deprived'),
         group = factor(group, levels = c('Most deprived', 'Least deprived')))

# a random sample of 30 LSOAs from each group
set.seed(48)
my_sample <- outer |>
  group_by(group) |>
  slice_sample(n = 30) |>
  ungroup()








The factor() function with levels fixes the order of the two groups. This means R will always calculate Most deprived minus Least deprived, so that a positive difference means higher NO2 in the most deprived LSOAs.






Before running any test, it is always a good idea to describe and plot the data first. Let us look at the mean and standard deviation of NO2 in both groups, and store the difference between the two means as obs_diff as we will need it again later:



R code

# group summaries
my_sample |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))


# A tibble: 2 × 4
  group              n  mean    sd
  <fct>          <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Most deprived     30  20.8  2.51
2 Least deprived    30  18.8  2.21

# the observed difference in means
obs_diff <- mean(my_sample$no2[my_sample$group == 'Most deprived']) -
  mean(my_sample$no2[my_sample$group == 'Least deprived'])
obs_diff

[1] 1.94


We can then compare the two groups visually with a boxplot:



R code

boxplot(no2 ~ group, data = my_sample,
        main = 'NO2 in Outer London (samples of 30)',
        xlab = '', ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')








Figure 1: NO2 in samples of 30 Outer London LSOAs from the most and least income-deprived fifths.





In our sample, NO2 levels are higher in the most deprived LSOAs. However, the two boxes overlap considerably, and last week we saw that sample means vary from one sample to the next. So could a difference this large also appear by chance, even if there were no difference between the two groups in the population?



Every hypothesis test starts with a null hypothesis (H0). This is the ‘nothing is going on’ explanation, against which we look for evidence. It comes with an alternative hypothesis (H1). For our question, these are:

H0: in the population, mean NO2 is the same in both groups, and any difference we see in our sample is due to sampling variability.
H1: in the population, mean NO2 differs between the two groups.

The test then answers one specific question: if H0 were true, how surprising would the data we observed be?



If H0 is true, the labels Most deprived and Least deprived do not tell us anything about NO2: any LSOA could just as well have had the other label. This gives us a simple way to see what chance alone can produce. We randomly shuffle the labels, calculate the difference between the two group means again, and repeat this thousands of times. This is called a permutation test, and we can run it with replicate(), which you used last week:



R code

# shuffle the group labels 5,000 times; each time, compute the difference
set.seed(48)
perm_diffs <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled <- sample(my_sample$group)
  mean(my_sample$no2[shuffled == 'Most deprived']) -
    mean(my_sample$no2[shuffled == 'Least deprived'])
})








NotePredict first



If the labels are shuffled at random, what do you expect the typical difference between the two groups to be?


Let us plot the 5,000 differences, together with the difference we actually observed:



R code

hist(perm_diffs, breaks = 40,
     xlim = range(perm_diffs, obs_diff, -obs_diff),
     main = 'What chance alone produces',
     xlab = 'Difference in mean NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Number of shuffles',
     col = 'grey80', border = 'white')
abline(v = c(obs_diff, -obs_diff), col = 'red', lty = c(1, 2))








Figure 2: Differences in means after shuffling the group labels 5,000 times. The solid red line is the observed difference; the dashed line is the same difference in the other direction.

text:

On the field trip to Catalonia, your group will collect its own spatial data: the route you walk, and the sites you record for your Urban Project. After the trip, in the mapping sessions, we will put these data on a map, combine them with other data, and turn them into a story map. Anything you do not collect in Catalonia cannot be collected afterwards, so this week is all about making sure that everything works before you travel.






ImportantBefore the session: set up and test walk



Please work through the Before the session section below. It takes about 20 minutes, most of which is spent walking. There is nothing to hand in, but do bring your phone to the session, with your test walk saved in Strava.








ImportantEvery working group has its own survey link



In Catalonia, your working group logs its sites with its own link to the field survey, which you find on the Field Survey Links page. The link fills in your fieldwork group and working group number for you, so that every site ends up with your group. Only ever use your own group’s link. The test link is only for signing in and testing, before and during the session.








NoteDoing your fieldwork in London?



This page is written for the field trip to Catalonia, but the same instructions apply to you. Wherever it says Catalonia, read London, and use the London links on the Field Survey Links page.




Almost everything geographers study happens somewhere. Spatial data record not only what something is, but also where it is. A photo of a street vendor is data; the same photo together with the coordinates of where it was taken is spatial data, because we can place it on a map and relate it to everything else around it: the route you walked, the neighbourhood it sits in, or the census statistics for that area.
Most spatial data take one of three basic shapes:

Points: a single location, such as a site you record or a bus stop.
Lines: a sequence of locations, such as the route you walk.
Polygons: an area with a boundary, such as a neighbourhood or a census district.

Locations are stored as coordinates: the latitude, which is the position north or south of the equator, and the longitude, which is the position east or west of the meridian through Greenwich. Plaça de Catalunya in Barcelona, for instance, is at about 41.387° N, 2.170° E. Your phone works out its coordinates using satellite positioning (GPS). Outdoors, this is typically accurate to within 5 to 10 metres, but the accuracy drops between tall buildings and indoors, which is worth keeping in mind when you record sites in narrow streets.
A geographic information system (GIS) is software for storing, combining, analysing and mapping spatial data. Because every record has a location, a GIS can overlay datasets that were collected separately, such as your sites, your route, a street map and census data, and help us answer questions about where things happen and what is near what. In this module, we will use ArcGIS Online, a GIS that runs in your web browser.



Your group will collect two datasets: your route as a line, and your sites as points. Each of these is collected with a different tool:

Next, we will make sure that you can open the field survey and sign in to it:

Check that your route looks right on the map, and take note of how much battery the walk used.

your phone, charged, with the test walk saved in Strava;
your Strava login details;
a note of anything that did not work, or that you were unsure about.

Try the field survey. Open the test survey and submit one test entry from the room:

Data collection and Working group number are already filled in as Fieldwork - Test and 0, and cannot be changed.
For Site ID, enter S00.
For Location, tap Allow when asked, and check that the dot on the map is roughly where you are. If it is not, wait a few seconds or drag it to the right spot.
For the photo and the short note, anything will do.
Tap Submit and check that you see a confirmation. 

Fix any problems. If something did not work, try to sort it out first with your working group and the students around you, using the troubleshooting table, which covers the most common issues. If you are still stuck, or have any other questions, ask the teaching staff for help.

By the end of this part, everyone should have exported a .gpx file and submitted one test entry from their own phone.






WarningSort it out now, not in Catalonia



Time in the field is limited, and you do not want to spend it on fixing settings, finding passwords or working out how the survey works. Anything that does not work today is much easier to fix here, with help at hand, than on a street corner in Catalonia.





Next, sit down with your working group and agree how you will collect your data once you are in Catalonia:

Who records the route. Choose one or two people to record the route in Strava. With two, you still have a route if one recording fails. These people will also export the route after the trip and share it with the rest of the group.

Who takes over. Agree who takes over the route recording or the site logging if one of these phones runs out of battery.
Which sites. Discuss what kind of sites you will record and how they relate to your Urban Project theme.

Finally, whoever logs the sites, and whoever takes over from them, saves your group’s survey link to their phone:

Open the Field Survey Links page, find your fieldwork group and working group number, and tap your group’s link.
Check that the top of the form shows your fieldwork group and working group number.
Add the survey to your home screen. In Safari, use Share → Add to Home Screen; in Chrome, use the ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen. Give it a name you will recognise, such as Survey WG05.
Open the survey from the new home screen icon, and show it to a member of the teaching staff before you leave the session, so that we can check together that it shows your group.
Close the survey without submitting anything. You will use it for the first time in Catalonia.





Once you are in Catalonia, there are a few things to keep in mind:

Whoever logs the sites opens the survey from the home screen icon you saved in the session, and submits one entry per site while standing at the site. Your fieldwork group and working group number are filled in for you, so you only add the site ID, location, photo and note.
Whoever records the route starts Strava when the group starts walking, and stops it when you finish. One recording per outing is fine, and you can have several recordings in total.
Charge your phone every night and bring a power bank if you have one, because GPS and the camera use more battery than usual.
If you have no signal or no mobile data, Strava will keep recording and upload your route once you are back online. The survey, however, needs a connection to submit. If you have none, take a photo with your camera, note the site ID and time in your notebook, and submit the entry later, placing the point by dragging the dot to the right location on the map.
Please be considerate. Survey entries will be public, because they appear in the story maps you publish later on. So do not take photos in which people’s faces can be recognised, do not put anyone’s name or other personal details in your notes, and follow the ethics guidance in your Urban Project worksheet. Do not record your accommodation as a site.







TipCheck your roaming charges



Before you travel, check whether your phone contract includes mobile data in Spain, and what it costs if it does not. If in doubt, switch off mobile data and rely on wifi: Strava records without a connection, and you can submit survey entries later.





Your sites will already be in ArcGIS Online, but there are two things to do before the next session:

Export and share the route. Whoever recorded the route downloads the .gpx file(s) from the Strava website, just as you did in the session, and shares them with the rest of the working group. If two people recorded, their routes should be the same, so one copy is enough; pick the one with the fewest gaps.
Share everything else. Put any extra photos, videos and notes in a shared OneDrive or Google Drive folder for your working group. It is best to avoid WhatsApp for photos, because it compresses them and removes their location information.

Check that location access is set to While Using the App with Precise Location on. Do not force-close the app while recording, and turn off Low Power Mode if the route has gaps.

title: 3 Building a Story Map
text:
Last week, you made a map of your group’s sites and route. This week, we will use that map as the centre of a story map: a web page, built in ArcGIS StoryMaps, that combines text, photos, video and your interactive map to tell a short story about your theme. A story map is also the format of the first GIS worksheet, so what you build in this session is the start of your submission.






ImportantBefore the session



Please make sure you have the following ready before the session starts:

your saved web map from last week, which you can find in Content → My content;
your group’s photos and any videos, downloaded to the laptop you will be working on (your group shares these in its own OneDrive folder);
the worksheet brief for this task. The brief sets out what your story map must contain; this chapter shows you how to build it.





A story map is a scrolling web page in which you can place a map right next to the text it belongs to. The reader scrolls through the story, and can also zoom, pan and click on the map. A good story map has a clear storyline, and every photo, video and map element is there because it supports that storyline.
For an example, have a look at Short revisit to the Cholera Outbreak in Soho, London (1854) by Dr Anwar Musah, who designed the original story map material for this module. It retells John Snow’s famous map of cholera deaths around the Broad Street water pump, and shows how text, images and an interactive map can work together. It uses different data and is longer than your story map can be, so use it for inspiration, not as a template.
Your story map must fit the theme your group was allocated for the Urban Project. It is worth planning the storyline before you start building, by asking yourself three questions:

What is the one thing you want a reader to understand about your theme in your study area?
Which evidence do you have for it: which sites, which photos, and which part of your route?
How will you split the story up? The worksheet limits the number of main sections, so decide what each section is for (for instance: the study area and aim, what you observed, and what you learned from the methods and the experience).

Write your headings down before you open the builder. This only takes five minutes, and it saves most of the time you would otherwise lose rearranging blocks.






NoteIf your screen looks different



ArcGIS StoryMaps changes its layout regularly. This chapter therefore describes what to click by its label. If a label has moved or been renamed, look for the closest equivalent, and ask in class if you cannot find it.





Let us start by creating a new story and setting up its cover:

Go to https://uclondon.maps.arcgis.com, sign in with UCL SSO, and open StoryMaps from the app launcher or the top menu.
Click New story. This opens the story builder, in which you write directly in the page and add content with the + button that appears between blocks.
Click on the title placeholder and type your main title. Keep it short and specific, and make it about your theme rather than something like “My story map”.
In the cover, add your candidate number and your fieldwork group and working group number (for example CAT1_WG05) as the subtitle. Please do not put your name anywhere: if your name is shown as the author on the cover, remove it in the cover settings.
Choose a cover design that suits your theme, and pick a cover image from your group’s photos. 

Your story is saved automatically as a draft in your own ArcGIS Online content.



To add text, click below the cover and start typing. Use Heading from the text style menu for each of your main sections, so that the story gets a clear structure and a navigation bar. Try to keep paragraphs short, because people read web pages differently from essays.
Write for a reader who was not on the trip. Your text should explain the aim, the place, and what you did and learned, in your own words. The worksheet sets the word limit.






NoteTry it yourself



Once your headings are in place, show only the headings to the person next to you. Can they tell what your story is about, and in which order it will unfold? If not, rework the headings before you write the text.





Next, we will add the web map you made last week:

Click + where the map should go and choose Map.
Select My content, choose the web map you saved last week, and click Add.
If you are asked about sharing, agree to share the map at the same level as the story. You will make the story public at the end (see Share and submit).
Use the map block’s Options to switch on the legend, the zoom buttons and the expand button (which lets the reader open the map full screen), and set the starting view to your study area.
Click on a point to check that the pop-up still shows the site ID, note and photo. 

If you would like the map to change as the reader scrolls through the text, you can try a Sidecar or Immersive block. These place the text in a panel that scrolls over a full-screen map. This is a nice extra, but it is not a requirement.






NoteThe map lives in two places



Your web map is a separate item from your story. If you change the map later, for example to restyle a layer, those changes will show up in the story automatically. Do not delete the web map or its layers before you have submitted.





Photos are where your story comes to life. To add one:

Click + → Image and upload a photo from your computer. If uploads are slow, resize large photos first.
Add a caption under every photo that says what it shows and why it matters for your story. If the photo comes from your group’s shared folder, mention this.
Add alt text, so that the image can be understood by someone using a screen reader. 

Choose photos that support your argument: five good photos that you refer to in the text are better than fifteen that only decorate the page.






NoteTry it yourself



For each photo you plan to use, say in one sentence why it is in your story. If you cannot, leave it out.





Short clips from the field can add atmosphere, or an interview, in a way that photos cannot. Adding a video works much like adding a photo:

Click + → Video.

title: 3 Building a Story Map
text:
A story map is a scrolling web page in which you can place a map right next to the text it belongs to. The reader scrolls through the story, and can also zoom, pan and click on the map. A good story map has a clear storyline, and every photo, video and map element is there because it supports that storyline.
For an example, have a look at Short revisit to the Cholera Outbreak in Soho, London (1854) by Dr Anwar Musah, who designed the original story map material for this module. It retells John Snow’s famous map of cholera deaths around the Broad Street water pump, and shows how text, images and an interactive map can work together. It uses different data and is longer than your story map can be, so use it for inspiration, not as a template.
Your story map must fit the theme your group was allocated for the Urban Project. It is worth planning the storyline before you start building, by asking yourself three questions:

What is the one thing you want a reader to understand about your theme in your study area?
Which evidence do you have for it: which sites, which photos, and which part of your route?
How will you split the story up? The worksheet limits the number of main sections, so decide what each section is for (for instance: the study area and aim, what you observed, and what you learned from the methods and the experience).

Write your headings down before you open the builder. This only takes five minutes, and it saves most of the time you would otherwise lose rearranging blocks.

title: 2 Mapping Your Field Data
text:
In Catalonia (or London), your working group recorded sites using the field survey, and recorded your route in Strava. This week, we will bring the two together on one map in ArcGIS Online. Everyone makes their own map. Next week, you will turn this map into a story map, so please make sure you save it at the end of the session.






ImportantBefore the session



Make sure you have a copy of your group’s route as a .gpx file, exported from the Strava website by whoever recorded it (see After the trip), and that you know your fieldwork group and working group number. You can look these up in your group’s link on the Field Survey Links page.




In Session 1, we saw that spatial data come as points, lines and polygons. A GIS keeps each dataset as a separate layer, and stacks these layers on top of each other to make a map. On our map, we will have three of them:

Your sites form a point layer, with one point per survey entry.
Your route forms a line layer: the track that Strava recorded.
The basemap at the bottom is the background (streets, satellite imagery, terrain) that gives your data context.

Each feature in a layer also carries attributes: the information stored about it, such as the site ID, note and photo you entered in the survey. In ArcGIS Online, you can see a feature’s attributes in its pop-up when you click on it. You can also use attributes to filter a layer, so that only some features are shown, or to style it, for instance by colouring points by category.
A map on a flat screen is always a projection of the curved Earth, which distorts distances and areas to some extent. ArcGIS Online takes care of this for us, so we will not need to worry about it in this module.






NoteIf your screen looks different



ArcGIS Online changes its layout regularly. This chapter therefore describes what to click by its label (e.g. Add). If a label has moved or been renamed, look for the closest equivalent, and ask in class if you cannot find it.





Let us start by signing in to ArcGIS Online and opening an empty map:

Go to https://uclondon.maps.arcgis.com, click UCL SSO, and sign in as you would for Moodle. Please use a laptop or computer for this, not your phone.
Open Map from the top menu. This opens Map Viewer with an empty map.
Take a moment to look around. The left-hand toolbar holds what is in your map (Layers, Add, Basemap, Save and open), whilst the right-hand toolbar holds the settings for the selected layer (Properties, Styles, Filter, Pop-ups). 




Click Basemap and try a few of the options. A quiet basemap such as Light Gray Canvas or OpenStreetMap makes your own data stand out, whereas Imagery shows what the places look like from above. You can change the basemap again at any time.



All field survey entries, from every group, are stored in a single layer. We will add that layer to our map and then filter it so that only your own working group’s sites are shown:

Click Add → Browse layers. Switch from My content to My organization, and search for UCL Geography Field Survey_results. Make sure you pick the layer whose name ends in _results: there are other items with a very similar name, which will not work. 
Click Add on the layer, and close the browse panel. The map will zoom to the points, and you will see the entries of the whole year.
In Layers (left-hand toolbar), click the survey layer so that it is highlighted. Then click Filter on the right-hand toolbar (the funnel icon), then Add new, and set up the following conditions:

Data collection is your fieldwork group (e.g. Fieldwork - Catalonia Group 1).
Click Add new again, and set Group number is your working group number. (In the survey this was called Working group number, but in Map Viewer the field is shown as Group number.)
Click Save. Only your group’s sites should now be visible. 

Zoom to your sites (in Layers, open the ⋯ menu of the layer → Zoom to) and click on a point. Its pop-up shows the attributes and photo your group entered.







NotePredict first



How many sites did your group log? Write the number down, then count the points on your filtered map. If the two do not match, check both filter conditions.


Note that the filter only changes your map: nobody else’s data are deleted or changed.



Next, we will add your group’s route from Strava:

Click Add → Add layer from file, and select your .gpx file.
When asked, choose to create a hosted feature layer, so that the route is stored in your own ArcGIS Online content. Give it a name such as CAT1_WG05 route (or LDN_WG03 route for London), and click Create and add to map. 
The route now appears as a line on the map. Check that it matches where you walked. If you have several recordings, you can add each .gpx file in the same way.




First, let us make the Layers list, and with it the legend, readable for someone else:

Give both layers a clear name, such as Survey sites and Route: open the ⋯ menu of the layer in Layers → Rename. This only changes the name in your map, not the original layer.
Check the order of the layers. The layer at the top of the list is drawn on top of the others. Because you added the route last, it is now on top, and may hide some of your sites. Drag the sites above the route by their handle (⠿).

To change how a layer looks, select it in Layers and click Styles on the right-hand toolbar. We will style both layers in turn:

For the route, keep the Location (single symbol) style, click Style options, and change the line colour and width so that the route is clearly visible on your basemap.
For the sites, change the symbol, size and colour so that the points stand out against the route. You could also style them by an attribute instead, but a single clear symbol is fine for now.

What we are aiming for is a map that someone who was not there can read at a glance: two clearly different layers, and nothing that distracts from them.






NoteTry it yourself



Switch between two or three basemaps now that your layers are styled. Which one works best with your colours, and why? Adjust your styling if needed.





By default, a pop-up shows every attribute in the layer, which quickly becomes cluttered. Let us tidy it up: click the sites layer in Layers, and then Pop-ups on the right-hand toolbar:

Set the title to the site ID by clicking on the title, typing {, and choosing the Site ID field.
Under Fields list, keep the fields that matter (site ID and note) and remove the rest.
Check that Attachments is included, so that the photo is shown.
Click on a few points on the map to check the result. 




Finally, we need to save the map so that you can open it again next week:

Click Save and open → Save as.
Use GEOG0187 – CAT1_WG05 as the title, with your own trip and working group number. Please do not add your name: the map ends up in your story map, which is marked anonymously. Add a short summary, for example Sites and route from fieldwork in Barcelona.
Click Save. The map will now be in Content → My content.

You do not need to share the map with anyone at this point.



By the end of this session, your saved map should have:

a basemap of your choice;
your working group’s sites, and only those;
your route as a line;
clear styling for both layers;
pop-ups that show the site ID, note and photo. 







NoteTry it yourself



If you finish early, estimate how far your group walked, and then check with the Measure tool (right-hand toolbar). You could also add labels with the site IDs (Labels on the right-hand toolbar): does this make the map easier or harder to read?








Problem
What to try




The survey layer does not appear in the search
Check that you are searching My organization, not My content, and that you signed in through UCL SSO.


No sites are left after filtering
Check that your filter uses exactly the same fieldwork group and working group number as your group’s survey link. If your sites are still missing, ask the teaching staff.


I do not have a .gpx file
Ask whoever recorded the route in your working group to share it. In the meantime, you can practise with the route from the live demonstration.


The .gpx file will not upload
Check that the file ends in .gpx and was exported from the Strava website. You could also try a different browser.


The route is a straight line or has big jumps
The GPS signal was lost during recording. If two people in your group recorded the route, use the other recording.


The photo does not show in the pop-up
Check that Attachments is switched on under Pop-ups. Note that not every entry has a photo.


I cannot find my map next time
Go to Content → My content, or search for GEOG0187.

title: 5 Describing Data
text:
In Term 1, you used R to describe data and conducted some basic statistical testing. Over the next three sessions, we will go back over some of this ground, but more slowly and with a clear purpose: to understand what the numbers mean, how sure we can be about them, and when a difference between groups is real. We will use one question throughout: who breathes the most polluted air in London? This week, we will set up a tidy workflow in R and use it to describe our data. This session and the next link to the first statistics worksheet.
The code is a means to an end. What matters is that you understand what each step does and why, so that you can tell whether a result makes sense. Throughout these sessions, we will therefore regularly ask you to predict a result before you run the code, and then check whether you were right.






ImportantBefore the session



Make sure R and RStudio are working on your laptop. You installed both in Term 1; if you run into problems, you can use Desktop@UCL Anywhere instead. Then run the following once in the RStudio console to install the tidyverse:
install.packages('tidyverse')




Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) mostly comes from road traffic, and long-term exposure is linked to asthma and other respiratory diseases. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that the annual mean should not exceed 10 µg/m³, with interim targets of 40, 30 and 20 µg/m³ for places that are still far above this guideline. The UK legal limit is 40 µg/m³. Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) comes from traffic, wood burning and many other sources, and has a WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³.
Air pollution is a physical phenomenon, but who is exposed to it is a social question. Researchers refer to this as environmental justice: are poorer neighbourhoods exposed to more pollution than richer ones? Over the next three sessions, we will describe, estimate and test exactly that.



We will be using a dataset that contains one row for each of London’s 4,994 Lower Super Output Areas (LSOAs): small statistical areas with, on average, about 1,500 residents. For each LSOA, the dataset contains the following variables:







Column
Description




lsoa_code, lsoa_name
LSOA code and name (2021)


borough, inner_outer
London borough, and whether it is in Inner or Outer London


population
Residents (mid-2022)


no2, pm25
Modelled annual mean NO2 and PM2.5, 2022 (µg/m³), averaged over the LSOA


imd_score, imd_decile
Index of Multiple Deprivation 2025: score, and decile within England (1 = most deprived 10%)


income_score
Share of residents who are income-deprived (0 to 1)



The NO2 and PM2.5 values are averages over whole LSOAs. No LSOA as a whole is above the UK legal limit, but many roadside locations within them are.






NoteData sources



Greater London Authority, London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory (LAEI) 2022, 20 m concentration grids, averaged per LSOA. Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025. LSOA boundaries: Office for National Statistics. All under the Open Government Licence v3.0.





Before we can load the data, we need to set up an RStudio project for the three statistics sessions:

In RStudio, go to File → New Project → New Directory → New Project. Call it GEOG0187-stats, save it somewhere sensible (not your Downloads folder), and click Create Project.
In the Files pane, click New Folder and create a folder called data.
Download the dataset and save it in that data folder:




File
Type
Link




London LSOA air quality and deprivation
csv
Download




Create a new script (File → New File → R Script) and save it as w05-describing.R. Type or copy the code from this page into your script, and run it line by line with Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Return on a Mac).







We will use the same project for all three statistics sessions, with one data folder and one script per week. If R tells you it cannot find the file, check that the project is open (its name is shown in the top-right corner of RStudio) and that the file is saved in the data folder under exactly this name.






In Term 1, you worked with base R: functions such as read.csv() and tapply(), and the $ operator. In these sessions, we will switch to the tidyverse: a collection of packages that share a common way of working. You take a dataset and pass it through a series of small steps using the pipe, |>, which you can read as “and then”. This is also how R is used in most Year 2 methods modules.
Let us start by loading the tidyverse and reading in the data. The glimpse() function gives us a first look at the dataset: the number of rows and columns, the type of each column, and the first few values.



R code

# load the tidyverse
library(tidyverse)

# read the data
lsoa <- read_csv('data/london-lsoa-air-quality.csv')

# a first look: rows, columns, types and first values
glimpse(lsoa)


Rows: 4,994
Columns: 10
$ lsoa_code    <chr> "E01000001", "E01000002", "E01000003", "E01000005", "E010…
$ lsoa_name    <chr> "City of London 001A", "City of London 001B", "City of Lo…
$ borough      <chr> "City of London", "City of London", "City of London", "Ci…
$ inner_outer  <chr> "Inner", "Inner", "Inner", "Inner", "Outer", "Outer", "Ou…
$ population   <dbl> 1795, 1671, 1896, 1737, 1837, 2961, 1761, 1859, 1719, 233…
$ no2          <dbl> 31.5, 29.7, 29.2, 30.3, 19.9, 21.5, 22.8, 21.3, 20.0, 20.…
$ pm25         <dbl> 11.04, 10.72, 10.63, 10.93, 8.88, 9.19, 9.64, 9.12, 8.92,…
$ imd_score    <dbl> 8.74, 4.72, 9.25, 19.88, 25.31, 37.22, 40.73, 39.15, 36.7…
$ imd_decile   <dbl> 8, 10, 8, 5, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2,…
$ income_score <dbl> 0.013, 0.018, 0.107, 0.211, 0.343, 0.486, 0.510, 0.403, 0…


The tidyverse is built around a small number of verbs, each of which does one thing. The table below lists the most important ones, together with their base R equivalents from Term 1:








Verb
What it does
Base R from Term 1




select()
keep some columns
df[, c('a', 'b')]


filter()
keep rows that meet a condition
df[df$a > 10, ]


mutate()
add or change a column
df$c <- df$a / df$b


arrange()
sort rows
df[order(df$a), ]


group_by() + summarise()
summarise per group
tapply(df$a, df$g, mean)


count()
count rows per group
table(df$g)



Let us try some of these. Each pipe below starts with the dataset and passes it through one or more verbs:



R code

# the five LSOAs with the highest NO2
lsoa |>
  select(lsoa_name, borough, no2) |>
  arrange(desc(no2)) |>
  head(5)


# A tibble: 5 × 3
  lsoa_name   borough   no2
  <chr>       <chr>   <dbl>
1 Camden 022A Camden   36.3
2 Camden 019E Camden   36.2
3 Camden 022C Camden   35.6
4 Camden 021C Camden   35.5
5 Camden 019D Camden   35  

# how many LSOAs in Inner and Outer London?
lsoa |>
  count(inner_outer)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  inner_outer     n
  <chr>       <int>
1 Inner        1966
2 Outer        3028

# LSOAs in Hackney with NO2 above 25
lsoa |>
  filter(borough == 'Hackney', no2 > 25) |>
  nrow()

[1] 39








NoteTry it yourself



Rather than writing new code from scratch, it is often quicker to adapt code that already works. Change the first pipe so that it shows the five LSOAs with the lowest PM2.5, and the last one so that it counts the LSOAs in a borough of your choice with NO2 above 20.


We can use mutate() to add new columns. Every LSOA in London is above the WHO guideline of 10 µg/m³, so instead we will flag each LSOA that is above the WHO interim target of 20 µg/m³. We will also divide London’s LSOAs into five equally sized groups (quintiles) based on income deprivation, from 1 (the least deprived fifth) to 5 (the most deprived fifth). Because we will use both new columns again, we save the result by assigning it back to lsoa:



R code

# add two columns
lsoa <- lsoa |>
  mutate(above_20 = no2 > 20,
         income_quintile = ntile(income_score, 5))

# check: about 1,000 LSOAs in each quintile
lsoa |>
  count(income_quintile)


# A tibble: 5 × 2
  income_quintile     n
            <int> <int>
1               1   999
2               2   999
3               3   999
4               4   999
5               5   998








Why do we use income deprivation rather than the overall Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD)? The IMD includes a Living Environment domain that partly measures air quality, so comparing NO2 with the IMD would partly mean comparing air pollution with itself. Using Income deprivation only avoids this problem.






When we describe a numerical variable, we usually report three things: its centre, its spread and its shape. We can calculate the most common summary statistics in one go with summarise().






NotePredict first



A few LSOAs have much higher NO2 than the rest (you saw the top five above). Do you expect the mean to be above or below the median? Run the code and check.





R code

# centre and spread of NO2
lsoa |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2),
            iqr = IQR(no2),
            min = min(no2),
            max = max(no2))


# A tibble: 1 × 7
      n  mean median    sd   iqr   min   max
  <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  4994  21.7   21.4  3.27   4.3  13.1  36.3



Centre: the mean is the average, and the median is the middle value. If the two differ a lot, the distribution is skewed or contains outliers.
Spread: the standard deviation (sd) is roughly the typical distance of a value from the mean, and the interquartile range (IQR) is the range covered by the middle 50% of values.
Shape: is the distribution symmetric or skewed, and does it have one peak or more? To see this, we need a plot.

For plotting, we will keep using base R, as in Term 1. Note that the $ operator still works on a dataset loaded with the tidyverse:



R code

# histogram, with the WHO interim target as a dashed line
hist(lsoa$no2, breaks = 40,
     main = 'NO2 in London LSOAs, 2022',
     xlab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Number of LSOAs',
     col = 'grey80', border = 'white')
abline(v = 20, lty = 2)








Figure 1: Distribution of annual mean NO2 across London LSOAs, 2022.











NoteTry it yourself



Proportions are means too. Because above_20 is either TRUE (1) or FALSE (0), its mean is the share of LSOAs above the interim target. Try running mean(lsoa$above_20). What does the answer tell you?




The mean we calculated treats every LSOA as one unit. However, LSOAs differ in the number of people who live in them, and if we want to say something about people, we should count people. A population-weighted mean does exactly that:



R code

# average LSOA vs average Londoner
lsoa |>
  summarise(mean_lsoa = mean(no2),
            mean_resident = weighted.mean(no2, population))


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_lsoa mean_resident
      <dbl>         <dbl>
1      21.7          21.8


In this case the two values are very close, but it is always worth asking yourself whether your unit of analysis is the area or the person.




We can compare groups by combining group_by() with summarise(), the tidyverse equivalent of tapply(). Let us compare NO2 levels in Inner and Outer London:



R code

# NO2 in Inner and Outer London
lsoa |>
  group_by(inner_outer) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))


# A tibble: 2 × 5
  inner_outer     n  mean median    sd
  <chr>       <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 Inner        1966  24.4   24.2  2.66
2 Outer        3028  20.0   20    2.31


A boxplot shows the median, the IQR (the box) and any outliers for each group side by side. The formula no2 ~ inner_outer can be read as “NO2 by Inner or Outer London”:



R code

# boxplot by group
boxplot(no2 ~ inner_outer, data = lsoa,
        main = 'NO2 by part of London',
        xlab = '', ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')








Figure 2: NO2 in Inner and Outer London LSOAs.





The same approach works for the boroughs. With 33 boroughs, it helps to sort the result, so that we can look at the boroughs with the highest and the lowest levels:

# borough summary, sorted by median NO2
borough_no2 <- lsoa |>
  group_by(borough) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            median = median(no2),
            iqr = IQR(no2),
            share_above_20 = mean(above_20)) |>
  arrange(desc(median))

head(borough_no2, 5)


# A tibble: 5 × 5
  borough                    n median   iqr share_above_20
  <chr>                  <int>  <dbl> <dbl>          <dbl>
1 City of London             6   30.7  1.55              1
2 Westminster              123   27.4  3.1               1
3 Kensington and Chelsea   101   26.6  1.7               1
4 Islington                126   25.8  3.17              1
5 Camden                   130   25.7  4.47              1

tail(borough_no2, 5)

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  borough                  n median   iqr share_above_20
  <chr>                <int>  <dbl> <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Harrow                 144   19    1.20         0.0972
2 Barking and Dagenham   115   18.7  1.60         0.157 
3 Bexley                 148   18.1  1.10         0.0405
4 Bromley                199   17.7  2.75         0.101 
5 Havering               153   16.1  1.5          0     





Let us now return to our environmental justice question, and look at NO2 levels for each income deprivation quintile.






NotePredict first



Which quintile do you expect to have the highest NO2, and do you expect a steady increase from quintile 1 to quintile 5?





R code

# NO2 by income deprivation quintile
lsoa |>
  group_by(income_quintile) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))


# A tibble: 5 × 5
  income_quintile     n  mean median    sd
            <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1               1   999  20.9   20.3  3.69
2               2   999  21.4   21.2  3.24
3               3   999  21.9   21.4  3.18
4               4   999  22.0   21.5  2.96
5               5   998  22.5   22.1  3.00


And plot the result:



R code

boxplot(no2 ~ income_quintile, data = lsoa,
        main = 'NO2 by income deprivation',
        xlab = 'Income deprivation quintile (1 = least, 5 = most deprived)',
        ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')








Figure 3: NO2 by income deprivation quintile (1 = least deprived fifth of London LSOAs).





It is worth looking carefully before drawing any conclusions. Is the pattern the same all the way from quintile 1 to quintile 5? Also remember that both deprived areas and polluted areas are more common in Inner London.






NoteTry it yourself



Repeat the summary within Inner and Outer London, using group_by(inner_outer, income_quintile). Before you run it, predict whether the pattern will still hold in both parts of London, and then check.








Describing is not the same as explaining. A difference between groups tells us that exposure is unequal, but not why: roads, housing, history and planning all play a part.






In a report, an essay or a worksheet, we describe our data in a short paragraph supported by a figure, rather than by copying R output. A good description covers:

what was measured, in which units, for which units of analysis (LSOAs, people), and how many;
the centre and spread, with suitable measures (median and IQR if the data are skewed);
the shape, shown in a figure that you refer to;
how groups differ, in numbers and in words, without claiming more than the data show.

Based on this session’s results, this could look as follows:

Across London’s 4,994 LSOAs, modelled annual mean NO2 in 2022 had a median of 21.4 µg/m³ (IQR 4.3 µg/m³), ranging from 13.1 to 36.3 µg/m³. Every LSOA was above the WHO guideline of 10 µg/m³, and 69% were above the interim target of 20 µg/m³. Levels were clearly higher in Inner London (median 24.2 µg/m³) than in Outer London (20.0 µg/m³).







NoteTry it yourself



Write a similar paragraph for PM2.5.





By the end of this session, you should have:

set up a project GEOG0187-stats, with the data in data/ and your script saved as w05-describing.R;
used select(), filter(), mutate(), arrange(), group_by() + summarise() and count();
described NO2 and PM2.5 (centre, spread and shape), with a histogram;
compared NO2 between groups, with a boxplot;
written two or three sentences that describe the data, as you would in the worksheet.

text:
When we describe a numerical variable, we usually report three things: its centre, its spread and its shape. We can calculate the most common summary statistics in one go with summarise().






NotePredict first



A few LSOAs have much higher NO2 than the rest (you saw the top five above). Do you expect the mean to be above or below the median? Run the code and check.





R code

# centre and spread of NO2
lsoa |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2),
            iqr = IQR(no2),
            min = min(no2),
            max = max(no2))


# A tibble: 1 × 7
      n  mean median    sd   iqr   min   max
  <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1  4994  21.7   21.4  3.27   4.3  13.1  36.3



Centre: the mean is the average, and the median is the middle value. If the two differ a lot, the distribution is skewed or contains outliers.
Spread: the standard deviation (sd) is roughly the typical distance of a value from the mean, and the interquartile range (IQR) is the range covered by the middle 50% of values.
Shape: is the distribution symmetric or skewed, and does it have one peak or more? To see this, we need a plot.

For plotting, we will keep using base R, as in Term 1. Note that the $ operator still works on a dataset loaded with the tidyverse:



R code

# histogram, with the WHO interim target as a dashed line
hist(lsoa$no2, breaks = 40,
     main = 'NO2 in London LSOAs, 2022',
     xlab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)', ylab = 'Number of LSOAs',
     col = 'grey80', border = 'white')
abline(v = 20, lty = 2)








Figure 1: Distribution of annual mean NO2 across London LSOAs, 2022.











NoteTry it yourself



Proportions are means too. Because above_20 is either TRUE (1) or FALSE (0), its mean is the share of LSOAs above the interim target. Try running mean(lsoa$above_20). What does the answer tell you?




The mean we calculated treats every LSOA as one unit. However, LSOAs differ in the number of people who live in them, and if we want to say something about people, we should count people. A population-weighted mean does exactly that:



R code

# average LSOA vs average Londoner
lsoa |>
  summarise(mean_lsoa = mean(no2),
            mean_resident = weighted.mean(no2, population))


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_lsoa mean_resident
      <dbl>         <dbl>
1      21.7          21.8


In this case the two values are very close, but it is always worth asking yourself whether your unit of analysis is the area or the person.

title: 5 Describing Data
text:
We can compare groups by combining group_by() with summarise(), the tidyverse equivalent of tapply(). Let us compare NO2 levels in Inner and Outer London:



R code

# NO2 in Inner and Outer London
lsoa |>
  group_by(inner_outer) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))


# A tibble: 2 × 5
  inner_outer     n  mean median    sd
  <chr>       <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 Inner        1966  24.4   24.2  2.66
2 Outer        3028  20.0   20    2.31


A boxplot shows the median, the IQR (the box) and any outliers for each group side by side. The formula no2 ~ inner_outer can be read as “NO2 by Inner or Outer London”:



R code

# boxplot by group
boxplot(no2 ~ inner_outer, data = lsoa,
        main = 'NO2 by part of London',
        xlab = '', ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')








Figure 2: NO2 in Inner and Outer London LSOAs.





The same approach works for the boroughs. With 33 boroughs, it helps to sort the result, so that we can look at the boroughs with the highest and the lowest levels:



R code

# borough summary, sorted by median NO2
borough_no2 <- lsoa |>
  group_by(borough) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            median = median(no2),
            iqr = IQR(no2),
            share_above_20 = mean(above_20)) |>
  arrange(desc(median))

1 Harrow                 144   19    1.20         0.0972

title: 5 Describing Data
text:
Let us now return to our environmental justice question, and look at NO2 levels for each income deprivation quintile.






NotePredict first



Which quintile do you expect to have the highest NO2, and do you expect a steady increase from quintile 1 to quintile 5?





R code

# NO2 by income deprivation quintile
lsoa |>
  group_by(income_quintile) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(no2),
            median = median(no2),
            sd = sd(no2))


# A tibble: 5 × 5
  income_quintile     n  mean median    sd
            <int> <int> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1               1   999  20.9   20.3  3.69
2               2   999  21.4   21.2  3.24
3               3   999  21.9   21.4  3.18
4               4   999  22.0   21.5  2.96
5               5   998  22.5   22.1  3.00


And plot the result:



R code

boxplot(no2 ~ income_quintile, data = lsoa,
        main = 'NO2 by income deprivation',
        xlab = 'Income deprivation quintile (1 = least, 5 = most deprived)',
        ylab = 'Annual mean NO2 (µg/m³)')








Figure 3: NO2 by income deprivation quintile (1 = least deprived fifth of London LSOAs).





It is worth looking carefully before drawing any conclusions. Is the pattern the same all the way from quintile 1 to quintile 5? Also remember that both deprived areas and polluted areas are more common in Inner London.






NoteTry it yourself



Repeat the summary within Inner and Outer London, using group_by(inner_outer, income_quintile). Before you run it, predict whether the pattern will still hold in both parts of London, and then check.








Describing is not the same as explaining. A difference between groups tells us that exposure is unequal, but not why: roads, housing, history and planning all play a part.

title: 4 Using Secondary Data
text:
So far, we have mapped data that you collected yourself. Most of the maps you will come across in geography, however, are made from secondary data: data collected by someone else, for their own purposes, and made available for others to reuse. This week, we will look at how to find such data, how to put them on a map, and how to decide whether they are fit for the question you want to answer. These are the skills behind the second GIS worksheet.






ImportantBefore the session



Sign in to ArcGIS Online with UCL SSO (see Open Map Viewer) and have a browser open. You will also need to know your fieldwork city: Barcelona if you went on the Catalonia trip, and London otherwise. Everyone does the same exercise, but with a different data pack.




Secondary data are produced by organisations such as statistical agencies, city councils, researchers or companies. Before you use any of them, you should find out five things. You will need the answers for your own referencing, as well as for the critical evaluation the worksheet asks for.







Question
Example




What does it measure?
Disposable household income per person (€)


Who produced it, and why?
Barcelona City Council, to monitor inequality


How was it collected or estimated?
Estimated from tax records and surveys, not a count of every household


When does it refer to?
Income in 2023


Where: for which areas?
1,068 census sections



You can usually find these answers in the dataset’s description or metadata page, which is one reason why you should always start there rather than with the map.



A choropleth map shades areas (polygons) by the value of a numerical variable, such as income, density or deprivation. Choropleth maps are easy to make, but they are also easy to get wrong, because each of the following choices changes what the map seems to say:

The variable. Use rates or averages (income per person, % of residents) rather than raw totals (total income). Otherwise, areas with more people will look “bigger” for no interesting reason.
The classes. The values are split into groups, each with its own colour. With equal intervals, the classes all have the same width; with quantiles, they all contain the same number of areas. The same data can look very different depending on which you choose.
The colours. Use a single-hue ramp from light to dark for values that go from low to high, and avoid rainbow palettes.
The scale. The same variable can look different for small areas than for large ones, because averaging over a large area hides the differences inside it. This is known as the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP).




Let us start by opening a new map (Map) and picking a quiet basemap. You can then follow the instructions for your city.






TipLeft, then right



Remember how Map Viewer is laid out. The left-hand toolbar holds what is in your map (Add, Layers, Legend, Save and open); the right-hand toolbar holds the settings (Styles, Filter, Pop-ups) for whichever layer is selected. So we always work in two steps: first click the layer in Layers so that it is highlighted, and then click the tool on the right. The name at the top of the right-hand panel tells you which layer you are changing.




For Barcelona, the data pack consists of three layers that we have prepared for you:

Click Add on the left-hand toolbar → Browse layers. Switch the drop-down at the top from My content to My organization, and search for GEOG0187 Barcelona.
Add GEOG0187 Barcelona - Census sections (income). This layer has one polygon per census section (the smallest statistical area), with the following attributes:

disp_income_pc_2023_eur: disposable household income per person, 2023;
mean_taxable_income_2024_eur: mean taxable income per unit of consumption, 2024;
gini_2024_pct: the Gini index of tax income, 2024 (a higher value means a more unequal distribution).

Add GEOG0187 Barcelona - Neighbourhoods and GEOG0187 Barcelona - Districts, which contain the boundaries of the 73 neighbourhoods and 10 districts. You will use these as context.



Open Layers and check the order. The layer at the top of the list is drawn on top of the others, so the census sections should be at the bottom, with the neighbourhoods above them and the districts at the top. If the order is different, drag the layers by their handle (⠿) on the left.







NoteData source



Barcelona City Council, Open Data BCN (CC BY 4.0), based on the Idescat income account and the INE Household Income Distribution Atlas. Sections, neighbourhoods and districts come from the Administrative units of the city of Barcelona dataset.





For London, we will use the official deprivation data, which are already available in ArcGIS Online:

Click Add on the left-hand toolbar → Browse layers. Switch the drop-down at the top to ArcGIS Online, and search for Lower Level Super Output Area (LSOAs) IMD2025 (WGS84) from gis@communities.gov.uk.
Add the layer. It contains one polygon for every LSOA in England (small areas of about 1,500 residents), with the rank and decile of the Index of Multiple Deprivation (2025).
To see only London, click the layer in Layers, then Filter on the right-hand toolbar → Add new. Set LSOA Name (LSOA21NM) starts with the name of a borough (for example Camden). You can add more conditions with or for any other boroughs you want to include.
For context, and to compare scales, also add Local Authority (Lower Tier) IMD2025 (WGS84) from the same publisher. This layer has one polygon per local authority, including the London boroughs (filter on LAD24NM). In Layers, drag it above the LSOAs, and give it no fill and a visible outline (see Compare scales for how).







NoteData source



Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 (Open Government Licence v3.0).






Now that the data are on the map, we can turn the main layer into a choropleth:

In Layers, click the main layer (the census sections, or the LSOAs for London), and then click Styles on the right-hand toolbar.
Under Choose attributes, click + Field and pick the numerical variable: disp_income_pc_2023_eur for Barcelona, IMDRank for London.
Under Pick a style, select Counts and Amounts (color) and click Style options.








NotePredict first



With Equal interval, every class has the same width; with Quantile, every class contains the same number of areas. In Barcelona, a few sections have much higher incomes than the rest. Which of the two do you expect to show most of the city in the same colour? For London, the variable is a rank: do you expect the two classifications to look different at all? Write down your guess before the next step.



In Style options, switch on Classify data. Under Method, try Natural breaks, Quantile and Equal interval in turn, and set Number of classes to 5 each time. Look at how the map and the class limits change. Was your guess right?



Choose a single-hue colour ramp. If the polygon outlines clutter the map, switch them off or make them thinner.
Click Done, and open Legend on the left-hand toolbar. Does the legend make clear what is being shown, and in which units? A name such as disp_income_pc_2023_eur does not. To change this, click Fields on the right-hand toolbar, and click on the field. In the panel that opens, type a readable Display name, such as Disposable income per person, 2023 (€). You can rename the layer itself via its ⋯ menu in Layers → Rename.

Finally, settle on one classification for your map and note down why you chose it: the worksheet asks you to justify this choice.



Next, let us see how much the picture depends on the size of the areas. For this, the boundary layers need to show only their outlines:

In Layers, click the neighbourhoods layer, and then click Styles on the right-hand toolbar.
A boundary layer has only one style, Location (Single symbol). Click Style options under it, and then the pencil next to Symbol style.
Next to Fill color, click the no colour button (the circle with a line through it, on the far right). Keep a dark Outline color.
Close the Symbol style panel and click Done.
Do the same for the districts, with a thicker outline (for example 2 or 3 px under Outline width), so that you can tell the two apart.



Zoom into one district.







NotePredict first



Do you expect income to vary more between neighbourhoods or within them, between the census sections of a single neighbourhood? Then compare a few neighbourhoods on the map and check.








NoteTry it yourself



If you are working with the London data, do the same with the boroughs. Compare the pattern of LSOAs within a borough with the single borough outline. Why might one borough-level summary hide a lot?





A good pop-up does more than just show numbers. Let us set one up for the main layer:

First, switch off the pop-ups of the boundary layers. Otherwise, clicking on the map opens the neighbourhood or district instead of the census section. In Layers, click the neighbourhoods layer, then Pop-ups on the right-hand toolbar, and switch off Enable pop-ups. Do the same for the districts (or the boroughs, for London).
Now click the main layer in Layers, and then Pop-ups on the right-hand toolbar.
Click Title and set it to the neighbourhood (Barcelona) or the LSOA name (London).
By default, the pop-up also contains a Fields list with every attribute in the layer. Remove it by clicking the ⋯ next to Fields list → Delete.
Click Add content → Text, and then Edit text. Write the value with a clear name and unit, for example Disposable income per person (2023): €{disp_income_pc_2023_eur}. To avoid typos in the field name, insert it with the {} button in the text toolbar rather than typing it.
Below that, add a short interpretive note: one sentence on what the value means in context. Click OK.
Click on a few areas to check the result.





To finish, choose one variable from your data pack and answer the five questions from Secondary data and where it comes from. Then think of two or three limitations of the data. The following questions can help you with this:

Scale: what is hidden when we show averages for areas?
Completeness: are there areas missing? In the Barcelona layer, mean_taxable_income_2024_eur is empty for three sections. Why might these data be missing?
Method: is the variable a count, an estimate or the output of a model? (The London index gives ranks: what does a rank not tell you?)
Time: does the data refer to the same year as your fieldwork?
Bias: who is more likely to be missing from, or poorly represented in, the underlying data?

Keep your answers as notes, because you will need them for the worksheet.



Save your map via Save and open → Save as, with a title such as GEOG0187 – Secondary data (without your name, as for the first map). You will build on this map for the second story map.



By the end of this session, you should have:

your main layer shaded by one numerical variable;
a context layer (boundaries) on the map;
a legend that explains the variable and its units;
a pop-up with a value and an interpretive note;
notes on the five questions and two or three limitations of your data.




For the worksheet, you do not have to use the data pack above. If you would like to find your own data, the following are good places to start:

ArcGIS Living Atlas, via Add → Browse layers → Living Atlas.
Open Data BCN (opendata-ajuntament.barcelona.cat) for Barcelona.
The London Datastore (data.london.gov.uk), the ONS (ons.gov.uk) and data.gov.uk for London and the UK.







WarningTables are not maps



Many datasets come as a table of values per area (for example, income by neighbourhood or by LSOA), with only the area’s name or code, and no boundaries. To map such a table, you would first need to join it to a boundary layer, which we do not cover in this module. So look for data that already include their geometry: a layer in ArcGIS Online or the Living Atlas, or a download offered as GeoJSON or a zipped shapefile, which you can add with Add → Add layer from file.


Whichever source you use, check the licence, and always record the name, publisher and year of the dataset for your references.






Problem
What to try




The Barcelona layers do not appear
Search My organization, not My content, and check that you signed in through UCL SSO. Let staff know if the layers are missing.


The London layer is slow or looks wrong
Apply the borough filter first, and then zoom in.


The map looks like it is all one colour
Check the classification and the number of classes, and try quantile.


The legend shows odd numbers
Edit the legend labels, or round the values in the style options.


Clicking the map opens a neighbourhood, district or borough
Switch off Enable pop-ups for the boundary layers (see Write the pop-up).


The boundary layers hide the colours underneath
Set their fill to no colour (see Compare scales), and check that they are above the main layer in Layers.


A value is empty in the pop-up
The data may be missing for that area. If so, mention this in your evaluation.

Finally, settle on one classification for your map and note down why you chose it: the worksheet asks you to justify this choice.

text:
Next, let us see how much the picture depends on the size of the areas:

Put the neighbourhoods and districts layers above your income layer, and set their fill to none with a visible outline.
Zoom into one district.

title: 4 Using Secondary Data
text:
A good pop-up does more than just show numbers. Let us set one up for the main layer:

First, switch off the pop-ups of the boundary layers. Otherwise, clicking on the map opens the neighbourhood or district instead of the census section. In Layers, click the neighbourhoods layer, then Pop-ups on the right-hand toolbar, and switch off Enable pop-ups. Do the same for the districts (or the boroughs, for London).
Now click the main layer in Layers, and then Pop-ups on the right-hand toolbar.
Click Title and set it to the neighbourhood (Barcelona) or the LSOA name (London).
By default, the pop-up also contains a Fields list with every attribute in the layer. Remove it by clicking the ⋯ next to Fields list → Delete.
Click Add content → Text, and then Edit text. Write the value with a clear name and unit, for example Disposable income per person (2023): €{disp_income_pc_2023_eur}. To avoid typos in the field name, insert it with the {} button in the text toolbar rather than typing it.
Below that, add a short interpretive note: one sentence on what the value means in context. Click OK.
Click on a few areas to check the result.

title: 4 Using Secondary Data
text:
To finish, choose one variable from your data pack and answer the five questions from Secondary data and where it comes from. Then think of two or three limitations of the data. The following questions can help you with this:

Scale: what is hidden when we show averages for areas?
Completeness: are there areas missing? In the Barcelona layer, mean_taxable_income_2024_eur is empty for three sections. Why might these data be missing?
Method: is the variable a count, an estimate or the output of a model? (The London index gives ranks: what does a rank not tell you?)
Time: does the data refer to the same year as your fieldwork?
Bias: who is more likely to be missing from, or poorly represented in, the underlying data?

Keep your answers as notes, because you will need them for the worksheet.

title: 4 Using Secondary Data
text: Save your map via Save and open → Save as, with a title such as GEOG0187 – Secondary data (without your name, as for the first map). You will build on this map for the second story map.

title: 4 Using Secondary Data
4 Using Secondary Data
text:
For the worksheet, you do not have to use the data pack above. If you would like to find your own data, the following are good places to start:

ArcGIS Living Atlas, via Add → Browse layers → Living Atlas.
Open Data BCN (opendata-ajuntament.barcelona.cat) for Barcelona.
The London Datastore (data.london.gov.uk), the ONS (ons.gov.uk) and data.gov.uk for London and the UK.







WarningTables are not maps



Many datasets come as a table of values per area (for example, income by neighbourhood or by LSOA), with only the area’s name or code, and no boundaries. To map such a table, you would first need to join it to a boundary layer, which we do not cover in this module. So look for data that already include their geometry: a layer in ArcGIS Online or the Living Atlas, or a download offered as GeoJSON or a zipped shapefile, which you can add with Add → Add layer from file.


Whichever source you use, check the licence, and always record the name, publisher and year of the dataset for your references.
